articles.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Trump's order comes after the trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.
Trump has repeatedly posted threats about renaming the lake, one of the five Great Lakes that straddle both countries, on social media amid the trade dispute.
He said on Thursday the move was "official, effective immediately" and that his administration has "filed all the necessary papers, documents" to make the change.

Text of the executive order says it gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the name Lake Ontario can be traced back more than 400 years, adding in a social media post on Thursday that preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he wrote. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario – today and forever."

When Trump took the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application. , external
In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.

There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters. While the US president has broad discretion over how his country officially recognises landmarks, other countries do not have to follow.
Canada does not have to recognise name changes made by other countries and officials there have dismissed the idea.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media, "It's Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever."
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston agreed, saying "We're into some real foolishness now. It's Lake Ontario, buddy."
"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," said Industry Minister Melanie Joly on Tuesday.

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.
As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it wasn't a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade".
Trump said he'd been thinking about renaming the lake "for a long time".
"So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," Trump said.
"Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."

The name change request comes amid a trade dispute that has seen US-Canada relations fall to new lows, with insults thrown back-and-forth between the Trump administration and Canadian officials over the past week.
There was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table sometime in the future.

Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said in a post on X that the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French "and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future US trade actions".
"We look forward to further constructive US clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty".
Trade talks collapsed at the last minute late on Friday night, with both sides accusing the other of demanding last-minute changes to a tentative deal.

Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic".
She wrote, "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect".

Other Democratic lawmakers in the US also criticised the order on social media, calling for the Trump administration to get back to negotiating on a trade deal. Some mocked Trump's idea and posted their own ideas to change the names of other landmarks.

Wisconsin's governor joked, "I just renamed Lake Michigan Lake Wisconsin," in a social media post with a video of himself signing a napkin on one of the Great Lakes. "See, I can sign napkins that say things, too," he added.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, "won't be calling it" Lake America.
Meanwhile, Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing, "We're on it, Mr. President!"

"The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA".

articles.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: Hundreds have died or are missing in Wednesday's flooding and landslides on the border of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.text: Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border
ByOlivia Ireland and Henry Moore
Massive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.
Search and rescue operations are continuing after Wednesday's disaster. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials describe "huge scale loss".
There are risks of more floods: a lake of rising water has formed at a site along the China-Nepal border - prompting fears it could burst its banks.
Here is what we know so far.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on Wednesday

blocks.text: Image source, Nepal Army via EPA
Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on Wednesday
What caused the deadly landslide?
Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating flood.
However, the US Geological Survey has clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.
The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event.
Debris flow from the collapse "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream" the USGS said.

blocks.caption: Map showing the path of floodwaters along the Lende Khola, Bhote Koshi and  Trishuli rivers in northern Nepal after a glacier collapse near the Tibet border. The collapse sent ice and rock debris into the river, triggering flooding that destroyed a border checkpoint and continued downstream past…

blocks.text: Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and, as rescue efforts continue, scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events.
Simon Cook, senior lecturer in energy environment and security at the University of Dundee who specialises in glaciology, said "climate change could have an impact".
Cook said his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.
He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.
He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".
Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet.
He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood."
One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.

Scientist will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.

A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu.
Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.
In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.
Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.
Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems.

In a report, the ICIDMOD said they are in the process of assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam - and a second flooding event.
Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockages.
Watch: BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is at a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopter
How many people are dead and missing?
The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear.
Nepali police say at least 389 people have died. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East.

In its latest update on Thursday evening, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 910 people were still missing. This included 517 foreign citizens, 44 members of the Nepal Army and 28 Nepal police officers.
Meanwhile, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday that the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558.
Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three.
The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 644 tourists were still missing, 33 of which were UK nationals, including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy.
It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.
The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal.

blocks.caption: Police officers carrying an elderly woman who survived the flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district of Nepal

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
How are governments responding?
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response.
China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.
In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance".

UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.
The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.
Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet border
What countries are the missing tourists from?
Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including:

items: India - the Nepal Tourism board says 288 nationals from neighbouring India are missing
China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal
US - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 65 US tourists are known to be among the missing
Ukraine - Ukraine's foreign ministry says 53 Ukrainian nationals are missing
Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say
Australia - Australia's foreign minister says 39 Australians are among the missing and there's an "unfortunate possibility" the number will rise
UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing
Canada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal says 24 Canadians are reported missing

blocks.text: Smaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.

articles.title: Coconut takes center stage this weekend
articles.summary: The humble coconut has long been part of the Filipino table, but there is much more to the fruit than gata, buko juice, and the other familiar staples. That broader potential is what the Department…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Food
The CoconutPhilippines Trade Fair enters its final weekend, showcasing Filipino coconut products and 300 MSMEs before the event wraps up Sunday
The humble coconut has long been part of the Filipino table, but there is much more to the fruit than gata, buko juice, and the other familiar staples.
That broader potential is what the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) is putting in the spotlight through the DTI–Bagong Pilipinas CoconutPhilippines Trade Fair, which ends this weekend.

The trade fair, which opened Aug. 26, brings together 300 micro, small, and medium enterprises working to develop products and find new markets for Philippine coconut products. For visitors, it offers a chance to discover what local businesses are creating from an ingredient that has long been part of everyday Filipino life.

There is good reason for the industry to be looking beyond the familiar. Philippine coconut exports rose 34.4 percent in 2025, reaching $3.6 billion, with the sector accounting for nearly half of the country’s total agro-based exports. It also supports 2.8 million Filipino farmers.
For DTI Secretary Ma. Cristina A. Roque, the opportunity lies not simply in harvesting coconuts, but in developing products that can create greater value for the people and communities behind them.

“The value of our coconut industry lies not only in what we harvest, but in what we create from it. We must maximize its potential by producing competitive, high-value products that generate lasting income for our farmers and local communities,” she said during the fair’s opening day.

The DTI is working to connect these enterprises with international buyers through export promotion, business-matching activities, outbound trade missions, and the Philippine Trade and Investment Centers’ global network.

There is also a wider push to open international markets for Philippine agricultural products. Cristina cited sustained overseas demand for bananas, pineapples, calamansi, and ube, while Philippine coconut exporters can also benefit from the country’s expanding network of free trade agreements, including the recently concluded Philippines-Chile FTA negotiations and ongoing discussions with the European Union and Canada.

For Filipino consumers, however, the most immediate reason to visit is simpler: there is only this weekend left to explore the fair. The CoconutPhilippines Trade Fair runs through Aug. 30, bringing together the participating enterprises and their products for those curious to see how a familiar Filipino crop is finding new expressions and new markets.

As Cristina put it: “The world already knows the exceptional quality of Philippine coconut products. Now, we must create more Filipino success stories that will bring better lives to our farmers and uplift communities nationwide.”
The fair runs through Sunday, Aug. 30, at the SMX Convention Center Manila in Pasay City.

articles.title: Jury deliberating in trial of Lindsay Clancy, US woman accused of killing her children
articles.summary: Prosecutors argued Clancy made a calculated decision to murder the children, while the defence argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

The fate of US mother Lindsay Clancy is now in the hands of a Massachusetts jury, who must decide if she is guilty of first-degree murder - the intentional and premeditated killing of another person - in the deaths of her three children.

For five weeks, the trial has gripped the country as Clancy's lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, who ranged in age from eight months to five years. Clancy does not deny killing her two sons and daughter.
The prosecution argued she made a calculated decision to intentionally murder them.
The jury could find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of lesser charges, or not guilty.
The jury of nine women and three men completed their first day of deliberations on Thursday. They will return on Friday.
In the state of Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory life in prison sentence without the possibility of parole.

The jury could instead find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or involuntary manslaughter - causing death because of extreme carelessness. Those convictions, too, would lead to some prison time.
If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, then she will not be set free, but instead sent to a psychiatric hospital, where she possibly could remain for life.
Attorneys for both sides made closing arguments on Thursday before the jury began deliberating.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's lawyer, repeated the defence's argument that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children with exercise bands at their home and then attempted to end her own life by jumping out of a window. Clancy was paralysed by the attempt and has attended the trial in a wheelchair.

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect," Reddington said, adding that he believed prosecutors were "not going to be able to prove otherwise".

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare and serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, and which should be treated as a medical emergency.

One of the more tense moments of the closing arguments came when Reddington directly addressed the prosecutors and asked them to explain why they tried to prove Clancy's suicide attempt was not serious. The judge interrupted and ordered him to address only the jury.
Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague did not dispute that Clancy was mentally ill, but told the jury that the defendant could tell the difference between right and wrong at the time of the killings.

"It's not the system or the DSM that caused her to strangle her kids," Sprague told the jury, referencing the US encyclopaedia of mental heath diagnoses, which does not give postpartum psychosis its own classification.
Sprague also said Clancy had an "abundance of care", but had hidden thoughts from doctors about harming her kids.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

articles.title: Allan Little: I met dangerously fanatical Mladić early in Bosnian war
articles.summary: BBC special correspondent Allan Little met the "Butcher of Bosnia" in the early months of the Bosnian war.

blocks.text: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.
BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war.
At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange.

You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations.
One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry.

Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning.
Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us.

The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall.
I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?"
The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years.
"I am," he said, "a musician".

Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children.

I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries.
You could buy a Kalashnikov for 200 dollars, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city.

I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting.

He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so.

In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically pure Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide.
Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way.

My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb.

We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing.
General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.

articles.title: Norwegians lay flowers at palace as King Harald's condition worsens
articles.summary: The 89-year-old's condition is described as "extremely serious" and members of his family have visited him in hospital.

blocks.text: Having been on the throne since 1991, King Harald is Europe's oldest head of state.
Crown Prince Haakon, 53, the successor to the Norwegian throne, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.

King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a condition that causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.

There was a sombre mood in Oslo as Norwegians followed the comings and goings of the royal family. Crowds milled around in Palace Square throughout the day as Norwegian public TV scrapped its schedule to cover the story.
Although no-one in the royal family spoke, the message was clear that it had become an important moment to visit the king.

Among those visiting the hospital were Crown Princess Mette-Marit who arrived with Haakon, as well as her son Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest during his appeal against a conviction for rape.
King Harald's sister, Princess Astrid, also visited the hospital, along with Haakon and Mette-Marit's children Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus.
Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre cancelled a planned trip to Germany, where he was expected to meet Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday.
"The whole nation is with us as we send warm thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family," he said in a statement.

articles.title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
articles.summary: Police have arrested a 19-year-old male suspect after an incident in which two people were killed near the German capital.

blocks.text: Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said.
Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used.
It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school.
One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported.
The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported.
Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide".
"The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger.
"I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said.
State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence".
The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday.
Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come.
"We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said.
A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added.
Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany.

articles.title: Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić dies aged 84
articles.summary: He was jailed for life in 2017 for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the wars in the ex-Yugoslavia in 1992-95.

blocks.text: Mladić - who never recognised the UN court - had been held at The Hague detention facility since 2011.
He commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.

During the war his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the main city of Sarajevo with the deaths of more than 10,000 people, and carried out the massacre of 8,000 men and boys at Srebrenica.

Hasan Hasanović , a Srebrenica survivor who lost his twin brother and father in the massacre, told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme that Mladić's death "does not bring closure because the people who were killed in Srebrenica cannot come back".

"His death is just a biological necessity, and it doesn't bring to an end the political project and military project that created that legacy of genocide. And we now live with the consequences of a divided country, genocide denial," said Hasanović, who now works at the Srebrenica memorial centre.
However, Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik told Reuters news agency that Mladić "was respected by Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs."
In Serbia's capital Belgrade, some local residents also praised him.
"I genuinely believe he protected the Serbian people, because after all, that was his duty," a man called Milan was quoted as saying by Reuters.
Another man, Vasilije, said: "It's a massive shame, it really is. Personally, I think it's a total injustice that he was even thrown in The Hague."

articles.title: What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow
articles.summary: There is nothing routine about John Ratcliffe making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow, writes Frank Gardner.

blocks.text: One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".

The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.
And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said.
News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally.

But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock.
Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.

Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy.
So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here.

These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them.

Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond.
In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5.

Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia.
If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours.

Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle.
Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger.

Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation.
Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else.
That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops.
But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

articles.title: Higher airfares ahead as CAB raises fuel surcharge in September
articles.summary: The local aviation industry continues to feel the pang of volatile jet fuel prices, as the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) is raising the fuel surcharge by a notch, resulting in slightly higher…

blocks.text: The local aviation industry continues to feel the pang of volatile jet fuel prices, as the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) is raising the fuel surcharge by a notch, resulting in slightly higher airfares.
In an advisory, the CAB said it is increasing the applicable surcharge rate to Level 13 for the period of Sept. 1 to 15 from the current Level 12.
Under Level 13, airlines may impose a surcharge of ₱423 to ₱1,237 for domestic flights and between ₱1,396.74 and ₱10,385.42 for international flights.
The exchange rate for airlines selling fares in foreign currencies is ₱61.39 to $1, the CAB said.
CAB is adjusting the fuel surcharge upward after jet fuel prices rose by 13 percent month-on-month to $163.87 per barrel as of Aug. 21.
Airlines are allowed to impose and collect a fuel surcharge from passengers as a way to recover financial losses caused by price hikes in jet fuel.
Given the volatility in the market, the CAB is adjusting the fuel surcharge level every 15 days, from the usual one-month coverage, to be more responsive to prevailing prices.
The upcoming increase in the fuel surcharge may impede travelers’ plans to book early flights for the upcoming holiday season, as airfares would become slightly more costly.
This comes at a time when passenger demand in the aviation industry is relatively stable and in need of some much-needed room for growth.
Based on the latest CAB data, the country’s passenger traffic from January to June increased by only one percent to 32.65 million from 32.25 million in the same period last year.
Broken down, international demand was the major driver of growth, increasing by nearly three percent to 15.27 million from 14.87 million a year ago.
Passenger traffic for domestic flights, on the other hand, remained steady at 17.38 million as airlines were forced to pause some routes due to higher fuel costs.
Against this backdrop, flag carrier Philippine Airlines (PAL) is raising its Manila-Melbourne operations from five times a week to daily flights beginning Nov. 19.
PAL said the expanded connectivity to Melbourne is in direct response to projected increased demand for the service during the holiday season.
PAL is working on expanding its international network as it looks to maintain its leadership in the segment against competition from low-cost carrier Cebu Pacific.
CAB data showed Cebu Pacific handled 3.41 million passengers by the end of June. PAL, meanwhile, ranked second with 3.39 million passengers.

articles.title: ₱7.2-trillion test: Can the House deliver an honest 2027 budget?
articles.summary: The filing of the proposed ₱7.2-trillion 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB), or House Bill No. 10858, presents the House of Representatives with more than another annual budget exercise. It is a…

blocks.text: The filing of the proposed ₱7.2-trillion 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB), or House Bill No. 10858, presents the House of Representatives with more than another annual budget exercise. It is a test of whether Congress has learned the painful lessons of the 2025 budget and the flood-control scandal—and whether it is prepared to restore public trust.

House Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Rep. Mikaela Angela “Mika” Suansing (1st District, Nueva Ecija) said the House may realign allocations among sectors and agencies as it sees fit. There is nothing inherently wrong with realignment. Congress has the constitutional authority and responsibility to scrutinize the executive’s proposed spending budget and improve it.
But the question is: Improve it for whom?

As congressmen deliberate on the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program, they must keep in mind that the ₱7.2-trillion budget is taxpayers’ money. Every peso carries the labor of a worker, the sacrifice of a family, the enterprise of a business, and the hopes of a citizen.
Therefore, the ₱7.2 trillion must serve the Filipino people—not political allies, favored districts, contractors, or private interests.

The proposed budget puts substantial resources into education, public works, health, local government, national defense, transportation, agriculture, social welfare and state universities. These allocations should translate into better schools, accessible health care, safer communities, productive farms, reliable infrastructure, and genuine opportunities for ordinary Filipinos.

The House must therefore treat every proposed realignment with suspicion—not because every amendment is corrupt, but because the experience of the 2025 budget demonstrated how opaque amendments can become fertile ground for abuse.

The flood-control controversy is a warning that Congress cannot afford to ignore. Senate investigations in 2025 uncovered allegations involving questionable, failed, and even “ghost” projects, while lawmakers themselves raised concerns over congressional insertions. Sen. Panfilo Lacson said congressional amendments are not necessarily illegal, but warned that large individual insertions can undermine properly planned government programs.

More troubling is the so-called “small committee,” where substantial changes to the budget could be made behind closed doors. Reports on the 2025 process described how this mechanism became another point at which alleged insertions could occur.
This is where the House must draw a bright and clear line.
No secret budget. No mystery amendments. No anonymous insertions. No political pork disguised as public spending.

If a lawmaker proposes moving billions of pesos from one agency or program to another, the public deserves to know who proposed it, why it was proposed, what project or program will receive the money, and what technical and fiscal basis supports the change.

Budget deliberations, including amendments and realignments, should be conducted in public through the appropriate House committees—or, when necessary, the plenary. The public should not have to rely on leaks, insiders, or investigations years later to discover where their money went.
Yes, open deliberations may take longer. But democracy is not supposed to be optimized for speed at the expense of accountability.
The House has an opportunity to make the 2027 national budget a genuine instrument of national development and social justice—from the poorest Filipino to the wealthiest.
The challenge is simple but profound: Will Congress merely pass the biggest budget in Philippine history—or will it produce one worthy of the people who pay for it?
The answer should be an honest-to-goodness budget, forged in the full light of day.

articles.title: A supportive LGU is key to a thriving agriculture industry
articles.summary: AVANT GARDENER What happens when an NGO’s project ends? If done well, it continues even without the organization’s supervision. I was invited to the End-of-Project Workshop of the International…

blocks.text: AVANT GARDENER
What happens when an NGO’s project ends? If done well, it continues even without the organization’s supervision.

I was invited to the End-of-Project Workshop of the International Institute for Rural Reconstruction’s (IIRR) and the International Development Research Centre’s AQUADAPT project, which supports the small farmer’s adoption of nature-based aquaculture as an additional source of income in the Philippines and in Cambodia.

You’ll notice that I’ve been writing a lot about IIRR. Before this, all of it came from a trip to Guinayangan, Quezon, upon the invitation of IIRR’s Senior Asia Program Advisor Dr. Julian Gonsalves, who I met at the International Plant Breeding Conference in celebration of UPLB’s Institute of Plant Breeding’s 50th Anniversary at the Manila Hotel in 2025.
I’ve been interested in IIRR’s work because it deals with factors specific to most of the Philippine agriculture landscape, i.e. small farms. In short, it works with culture and not against it.

“[The project explored] how small-scale agriculture can become a more resilient, sustainable, and viable life in options for rural communities in the face of a challenging climate," said Ermita Monville Oro, IIRR’s Acting Asia Regional Director. “Just as importantly, the project has brought attention to the critical role of women in agriculture value chains.”
What interested me most about IIRR is its insistence that the local government be involved in all their projects to ensure its continuous adoption even after the project ends.

The program included a panel with three government officials from its Philippine sites: Hon. Mayor Lovell Anne Yu-Castro of Alangalang, Leyte; Municipal Agriculture Officer of Guniyangan, Quezon William Lopez Jr.; and Municipal Agriculture Officer of Hingyon, Ifugao Andy Dimoc, who all answered the question that, given the end of the project, “What would be needed to make this approach sustainable at the local level?”
Yu-Castro discussed how a lawmaker can implement a program past their term by using AQUADAPT as an example.

“We have seen the success stories of our farmers. This project is evidence based,” she said in Taglish. “What I'm thinking is for us to institutionalize AQUADAPT implementation in our programs, in our PPAs (Public-Private Partnerships). We will be institutionalizing the AQUADAPT budgeting, the program implementation in our agricultural development programs… We will make it an ordinance so that even with the change in local officials, the support for AQUADAPT will stay. It will always be supported because this program will be institutionalized in Alangalang. We’re going to do that with the help of IIRR and our representative from MAO.”

Dimoc agreed, adding that participant ownership and a definite delineation of responsibilities among partner farmers and organizations are also important. “I think that this is really needed, especially if we are going to use the government funds in all these nature-based solutions programs. And those ordinances should have… funds their own. In our (area), we have a memorandum of agreement with our partner organizations, with our farmers, so that at least this is binding to both parties, I think, because they do this and responsibilities will be spelled out, so they know what are their duties and responsibilities, and also on our end, we know also our duties and responsibilities as partner LGUs,” he said.

Lopez, whose work in Guinayangan I will be writing about in a later column, echoed Yu-Castro’s sentiment by emphasizing the importance of a mayor who is heavily invested in the growth of their municipality’s various agriculture industries.

“To sustain this program, we are planning to enhance the nursery and we will make it a learning site so that the other aquaculture farmers, they will learn in our local municipality,” he said, explaining that in Gunayangan, LGU support came in the form of two fishery technicians for program monitoring and evaluation, the allotment of part of the annual budget to the development of the program, the enhancement of their municipal hatchery, and the development of an organic tilapia feed production program.

“We are planning to provide an adequate source of water for the rice-tilapia-based aquaculture [in coordination with the] National Irrigation Association,” he added. “We also intensified the seaboard patrolling, since we have 15 barangays coastal areas. Before, we were focused on marine monitoring for illegal fishing, but because of the AQUADAPT, we've also monitored the mangrove areas and the conservation of the species.”

The panel’s experiences show that local government cooperation and support is an extremely important factor in determining the longevity and continuation of NGO-led small-scale farmer programs, especially after these programs end. After all, the proof of an NGO’s effectiveness is when a community doesn’t need them anymore.

articles.title: 175 years of putting customers first
articles.summary: By BPI PRESIDENT AND CEO TG LIMCAOCO One hundred seventy-five years is an extraordinary milestone, and one that carries both pride and responsibility. Very few institutions have had the privilege of…

blocks.text: By BPI PRESIDENT AND CEO TG LIMCAOCO

One hundred seventy-five years is an extraordinary milestone, and one that carries both pride and responsibility. Very few institutions have had the privilege of serving generations of Filipinos through life’s most important moments, helping them save, build businesses, and achieve their dreams.

For BPI, our anniversary is more than a celebration of longevity. It is an opportunity to reflect on a simple question: what allows an institution to remain relevant for nearly two centuries? Many would point to innovation. Others would point to resilience. I believe it begins with something even simpler: an unwavering focus on the customer.

When BPI was established in 1851, the Philippines looked very different. Banking was conducted through ledgers, handwritten records, and face-to-face conversations. Since then, we've witnessed enormous changes—not only in banking, but in the country itself.

Yet despite all those changes, one truth has remained constant: people don’t aspire for financial products. They aspire for what those products make possible — starting a business, buying a home, educating their children, recovering from setbacks, and building a more secure future. Understanding that difference has shaped BPI for 175 years. It continues to shape how we serve our customers today.
That's why one of the things I often tell our teams is this: People don't really want a bank. They want a simpler, better life. That perspective has shaped every major chapter of BPI's history.

When we introduced modern banking to the Philippines, it wasn't simply about bringing new financial services to the country. It was about helping Filipinos participate in a growing economy. When we pioneered ATM banking, the goal wasn't to showcase new technology. It was to give customers access to their money beyond traditional banking hours. When we embraced digital banking, the objective wasn't to become more digital for its own sake. It was to make banking faster, more convenient, and more accessible. Today, that same thinking guides our investments in agency banking, allowing us to bring banking services closer to communities where convenience means something different for every customer.

Looking back, it's easy to celebrate these milestones as moments of innovation. I see them differently. They are moments of listening. Each innovation began with the same question: How can we make life better for our customers?
The answers have changed over 175 years. The question never has. That mindset has become even more important today.

Artificial intelligence is transforming industries. Digital payments happen in seconds. Financial services are becoming increasingly connected. These advances are exciting, and they hold tremendous promise for expanding financial inclusion and improving customer experiences. But technology alone does not create meaningful innovation. Innovation begins with understanding people. Technology is an enabler. Trust is the foundation.
The institutions that will thrive in the future won't necessarily be those with the newest technology. They will be those that know their customers best and continuously evolve alongside them.
But customer obsession isn't built through strategy alone. It's brought to life by people.

For 175 years, generations of BPI employees have been the face of that commitment. Every account we open, every loan we approve, every payment we process, every investment we recommend, every digital solution we build, and every concern we resolve is more than a banking transaction. It is an opportunity to make someone's life a little easier, a little better, and a little more secure.

Looking ahead, I have no doubt that banking will continue to evolve. The possibilities are immense. But I also believe that the next breakthrough in banking won't simply come from a new technology. It will come from listening more closely, understanding more deeply, and responding more thoughtfully to the people we serve.
As we celebrate BPI's 175th anniversary, we're proud of the milestones we've achieved. More importantly, we're grateful for the trust that generations of Filipinos have placed in us.

That trust has been our greatest privilege. It has also been our greatest responsibility. And it is why, after 175 years, our most enduring competitive advantage isn't simply our history. It is our commitment to continuously earning the right to serve our customers, today and for generations to come. In doing so, we fulfill our purpose of building a better Philippines—one family, one community at a time.

articles.title: Time to shine for Gilas locals
articles.summary: EDITORS DESK Today, Aug. 28, 2026, Gilas Pilipinas makes a crucial home stand against the visiting Jordan team at the Mall of Asia Arena in Pasay City. Two days later, it’s Gilas versus Iran. On the…

blocks.text: EDITORS DESK
Today, Aug. 28, 2026, Gilas Pilipinas makes a crucial home stand against the visiting Jordan team at the Mall of Asia Arena in Pasay City.
Two days later, it’s Gilas versus Iran.

On the surface, it is all about earning a spot in the 2027 FIBA World Cup set in Qatar. There is also the bigger goal, with the centerpiece event awarding top finishers from each continent a precious ticket to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

While it is paramount that the Nationals be able to secure more victories to better their 2-4 win-loss record and get a fighting chance in their group come two more windows in November and February of next year, there lies a problem that is wrapped like a gift for the future of our national team.
No Justin Brownlee, no Bennie Boatwright, no Ange Kouame, no Jordan Clarkson.

While it holds true value that these naturalized players offer the firepower, ceiling, the tenacity, and steely nerves for our team on any given situation, this showcase against the Middle East giants could give this basketball-crazed country a glimpse of future in its most bare, natural, all-Filipino form.
Time is now for the local cast to step up and show the crowd the resolve they have in critical situation.
The Nationals are playing the August window without their most dependable and consistent player in Justin Brownlee.
Brownlee, who was supposed to make his comeback after sustaining a myriad of injuries from his hamstring to his knees, won't be able to suit up for Gilas this weekend as he recovers in the US.
The 38-year-old forward was also absent when the national team played New Zealand and Australia last July.

Former San Miguel import Bennie Boatwright was a candidate to become a naturalized Filipino, but his papers won't make it in time with his documents now stuck in the Senate that is busy handling the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Ange Kouame could have been someone to be tapped in, but the 6-foot-10 center is still under his basketball contract in France.
Jordan Clarkson was floated, but there is so much needed to get his services as he is a certified NBA star.

These challenges pose a big threat to our national team's ambition of advancing to the World Cup, and these are the same hurdles the Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas should face when another all-Filipino crew plunges into action in the Asian Games where the country is the defending men's champion.
Without them, it sounds scary. But without them opens up the opportunity for the locals to further shine.

Minutes will be diverted to young guns Carl Tamayo, Kevin Quiambao and Dwight Ramos. Crucial shots could be handed to CJ Perez or Scottie Thompson. Defense is as agile and tall with Kai Sotto and June Mar Fajardo manning the paint.
When one is absent, everyone steps forward.
And this could be the stage of proving each one's worth when everything is on the line.
Above all, the crowd will be satisfied: this is all-Filipino.
(Ramon Rafael Bonilla is the editor of Manila Bulletin's Sports section.)

articles.title: Beyond disaster response: Redefining resilience
articles.summary: METRO MATTERS Every year, cities from all across the country face the challenge of mitigating disaster risks amid worsening global climate conditions. It is my mandate as mayor of the City of San…

blocks.text: METRO MATTERS

Every year, cities from all across the country face the challenge of mitigating disaster risks amid worsening global climate conditions. It is my mandate as mayor of the City of San Juan, president of the Metro Manila Council, and national president of the League of Cities of the Philippines to maximize government efforts to partner with the private sector to ensure the safety of Filipinos.

San Juan City is not exempt from the effects of these natural calamities as heavy rains continue to pour especially during the Southwest monsoon season. Yet despite the heavy downpour from Aug. 5 to 9, our preparations helped keep flooding in the city to a minimum, with no reported evacuations even in our low-lying areas.

On Aug. 10, when the rain continued to pour heavily and persistently, flood levels rose, but they were no longer as high as what we experienced in the past. We have seen significant improvements, but we also recognize the work that still needs to be done.
This was not the result of a single intervention. It was the product of months of dredging, sustained drainage cleaning and waste management programs all throughout the city.

We launched our search for the Cleanest Barangay, with the winner receiving ₱200,000, the 1st runner-up receiving ₱100,000 and the 2nd runner-up receiving ₱50,000, to encourage communities to work together and strengthen their environmental awareness and initiatives. We also amended our local ordinance to increase the penalty for improper waste disposal to ₱5,000, regardless of whether it is a first, second or third offense, as a deterrent. Through a resolution of the Metro Manila Council, we have encouraged similar efforts across the National Capital Region. But no government program can succeed without the discipline and genuine sense of stewardship of our communities. We are fortunate to have citizens who heed our calls and actively help us keep our waterways clean.

Still, preparation for the next disaster cannot stop with immediate response and routine maintenance. We must also address the long-term causes that contribute to flooding. Waste management is one of these challenges. As our cities continue to grow, we need solutions that are sustainable.

In my capacity as president of the Metro Manila Council, I have welcomed dialogues on alternative waste management methods, including the possibility of converting waste to energy. We are currently reviewing proposals and studying this technology to determine how it can be responsibly and effectively adapted to our cities’ needs.
Building resilience means investing not only in infrastructure, but also in our people and our environment.

Under our Makabagong San Juan administration, we continue to pursue projects to strengthen the city’s long-term flood resilience. We are constructing a new pumping station along F. Manalo Street in Barangay Batis and another one near the San Juan River. We have also purchased mobile pumps that can be deployed to different locations depending on necessity.

With the help of the national government, we are improving our drainage systems in various barangays. I have also met with my colleagues from other local government units in Metro Manila to discuss how we can consolidate our efforts as an interconnected region, because disaster preparedness and response cannot stop at city boundaries.
Resilience must also begin at home.

Last Aug. 12, we started distributing Emergency Go Bags to District 1 barangays, with District 2 following the day after. Each Go Bag contains basic survival items such as a hard hat, waterproof poncho, rechargeable flashlight, power bank, basic disaster preparedness handbook, and first aid kit. Our goal is to provide these to all 45,000 San Juan households by the first quarter of 2027. We continue to strengthen disaster preparedness in San Juan, making it a constant part of how we protect our communities, not just a response when a storm is approaching.

We are privileged to have a strong and mutually beneficial partnership with the private sector. I want to express my gratitude to Mr. Ramon Ang and San Miguel Corporation for their assistance in dredging the San Juan River, Maytunas Creek, and Ermitaño Creek at no cost to the city under Oplan Kontra Baha of our Bagong Pilipinas Administration. Our continued partnership with SMC, together with the support of the national government and the cooperation of our local communities, proves that we can better serve our people when we work hand-in-hand.

The challenges brought about by climate change remind us that resilience cannot be built by one city or one institution alone. It requires sustained preparation, responsible citizenship, strong partnerships, and investments that will protect our communities for years to come. This is the responsibility we share as local governments: to prepare before disaster strikes, protect our people when it does, and build a nation where no Filipino is left behind.

articles.title: Five were wise
articles.summary: REFLECTIONS TODAY Jesus’ question, “Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant?” in the parable of the Faithful Servant (Mt 24:45), should now be read, “Who then is the faithful and wise virgin?”…

blocks.text: REFLECTIONS TODAY

Jesus’ question, “Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant?” in the parable of the Faithful Servant (Mt 24:45), should now be read, “Who then is the faithful and wise virgin?” Going by the parable, the wise virgins are those whose eyes are open to what is yet to come; they do not simply live for the day. Christ will return and ask us for an accounting of our life.

The wise prepare for it beforehand. Here, they are symbolized by the five virgins who provide themselves with enough oil. The foolish are those who do not think of the future, do not prepare for it, and miss opportunities given them. They think that conversion is always possible at the last moment, or that they can always rely on others to rescue them from their predicament. Even as we do not know the day or the hour when we will meet the Lord, so we must always be prepared.

We cannot borrow someone else’s faith or grace at the last minute; we must cultivate our own. Like the wise virgins, we must have the foresight to bring extra oil—with spiritual readiness by living in the state of grace, continually nurturing our relationship with God through prayer, the sacraments, and acts of love and charity. We must ditch lethargy, laziness, and indifference so that we will not be found wanting when we face the Lord.
Gospel • Matthew 25:1-13

Jesus told his disciples this parable: “The Kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish and five were wise. The foolish ones, when taking their lamps, brought no oil with them, but the wise brought flasks of oil with their lamps. Since the bridegroom was long delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep.

“At midnight, there was a cry, ‘Behold, the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’ Then all those virgins got up and trimmed their lamps. The foolish ones said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ But the wise ones replied, ‘No, for there may not be enough for us and you. Go instead to the merchants and buy some for yourselves.’ While they went off to buy it, the bridegroom came and those who were ready went into the wedding feast with him. Then the door was locked. Afterwards the other virgins came and said, ‘Lord, Lord, open the door for us!’ But he said in reply, ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.’ Therefore, stay awake, for you know neither the day nor the hour.”
Source: “365 Days with the Lord 2026,” St. Paul’s, 7708 St. Paul Rd., SAV, Makati City (Phils.); Tel.: 632-895-9701; E-mail: [email protected]; Website: http://www.stpauls.ph.

articles.title: NNIC turning 2
articles.summary: A little over two weeks from now, San Miguel Corp. (SMC) Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ramon “RSA” S. Ang and his New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) team will be celebrating their second year of…

blocks.text: A little over two weeks from now, San Miguel Corp. (SMC) Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Ramon “RSA” S. Ang and his New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) team will be celebrating their second year of managing and upgrading the country’s premier airport.

As the saying goes: time flies when you’re engrossed, immersed, and focused on the task at hand—providing ease and comfort for both inbound and outbound passengers, as well as welcoming relatives and well-wishers.

Even before turning two this Sept. 14, NNIC (as of end-July this year) has already remitted some ₱78 billion, representing the national government’s 82.16 percent revenue share. That amount includes the ₱30 billion upfront payment.
Yes, Virginia, the renovations, changes, and upgrades at NAIA have reached a fever pitch, with the NNIC team successfully navigating and managing active operational constraints.

I saw this firsthand when I joined former Transportation Secretary and newly elected SMC independent board director Jaime “JJB” J. Bautista for a special tour showcasing the progress of the Terminal 3 renovations.

As a passenger, it was satisfying—delightful, even—to see the improvements NNIC has undertaken at the multi-level terminal, bringing significant upgrades to dining, boarding bridges, and passenger lounges.
Under the skillful management of NNIC Vice President for Commercial Operations Cecile Ang, underused spaces were converted into comfortable dining and retail hubs.

For this foodie, it’s comforting to note the wide variety of local and international dining options available in International Departures and at the Tambayan Food Hall, a waiting area for welcomers and well-wishers.
Shake Shack, Wildflour, Cibo, Conti's, Ramen Nagi, Lechon Diva, Starbucks Reserve, and the highly sought-after Estrel’s Specialty Bakeshop are among the notable additions.

I heard that Estrel’s business is thriving in T3, as folks in the southern part of the metropolis no longer have to traverse chaotic roads and endure the long drive to Quezon City for its caramel-iced chiffon cake, which, I believe, gives Hizon’s a real run for its money (and its cake).

Taking cognizance of the vital role played by the country’s unsung heroes, our overseas Filipino workers, whose dollar remittances pump up our current account position—NNIC has allocated a special lounge for them with ample seating, a relaxing ambiance, phone-charging stations, and, of course, free food and drinks.

The OFW Lounge is operated by the Department of Migrant Workers through its attached agency, the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA), which protects and promotes the well-being of OFWs and their families. Earmarking ₱10 million a month for maintenance, the lounge can accommodate 216 passengers.

But wait, Virginia, there’s more! For those with delayed flights, sleeping quarters are available with a capacity for 26 people—14 for men and 12 for women—replete with toiletry kits and shower rooms for freshening up.

Business-class passengers, on the other hand, can while away the time at the First Meridian Lounge. This 2,600-square-meter shared premium facility serves Emirates, Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines, Thai Airways, KLM, and Vietnam Airlines. It features a full-service bar, hot and cold buffets, a bakery section, a playroom, and an infant care section.
According to a Meridian staff member, the virtual golf simulator is the most popular amenity and is almost always booked.

Beyond terminal aesthetics, ongoing and pipeline project upgrades include the phased rehabilitation of passenger boarding bridges and fixed bridges, the installation of new escalators, and the construction of Terminal 5—set for completion around 2028—which will be dedicated to Philippine Airlines and AirAsia domestic operations.

Exploring the expanse of the 183,000-square-meter T3 complex, I observed an aura of delight and satisfaction from JJB and the NNIC team. In 2025, UK-based Project Finance International recognized the long-overdue rehabilitation of the country’s premier airport through a public-private partnership, naming it the “Transport Deal Award of the Year.”
Although much remains to be done, NAIA T3 has earned its mark and is now ranked 7th globally for having the highest number of food and beverage outlets per million passengers.
Way to go, NNIC! A salute to RSA and your team.
Talk back to me at [email protected]

articles.title: Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor Peter Cullen dies
articles.summary: Cullen voiced the heroic Optimus Prime in the Transformers TV series and then the Hollywood films.

blocks.text: His Optimus Prime voice was inspired by his older brother, a decorated US Marine and Vietnam War veteran, who suggested he should play the character as "a real hero, don't be a Hollywood hero".
"He said, 'Don't go yelling and screaming. He's strong enough to be gentle.'
"And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime."
Cullen gave his brother a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his death.

The actor's performance as the character earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children's & Family Emmy Awards in 2023.

Cullen's other roles included Monterey Jack in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, and he voiced characters in 1980s and 90s animated series including Spider-Man, Donkey Kong, Alvin & the Chipmunks, Dungeons & Dragons, My Little Pony, Duck Tales and Gummi Bears.

articles.title: UP needs fresh funding for NOAH
articles.summary: The University of the Philippines is seeking fresh funding in the 2027 national budget for Project NOAH, the core component of the UP Resilience Institute responsible for developing hazard maps that…

blocks.text: The UPRI received P1 billion this week from the Department of Budget and Management for Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards). It was earmarked in the 2026 budget after the government cut P255 billion from the Department of Public Works and Highways budget in the aftermath of the flood control scandal.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The University of the Philippines is seeking fresh funding in the 2027 national budget for Project NOAH, the core component of the UP Resilience Institute responsible for developing hazard maps that policymakers and the public use to plan for weather events.

The UPRI received P1 billion this week from the Department of Budget and Management for Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards). It was earmarked in the 2026 budget after the government cut P255 billion from the Department of Public Works and Highways budget in the aftermath of the flood control scandal.
The UPRI will use the mon- ey to upgrade its equipment, enhance hazard maps and fund research endeavors.
But the 2027 National Ex- penditure Program, for now, contains no new money for Project NOAH
The university pointed out that its funding in the 2026 budget was finalized only uring the bicameral conference committee.
UPRI executive director Mahar Lagmay said the P1 billion is “a good start,” but is not enough to execute all the plans they have in mind.
However, it’s a marked improvement from 2017 when NOAH was transferred to the UPRI.

Project NOAH had an annual budget of only over P30 million at the time, which it used to help cities craft their flood control master plans.With the huge increase in NOAH’s budget, Lagmay lai out the UPRI’s priority spending areas: high-resolution mapping of major river basins, support for the government’s Oplan Kontra Baha, simulation of major detention basins, drone surveys with state colleges and universities, native-tree mapping, sediment erosion and delivery assessment, mapping hidden waterways, promotion of nature-based solutions and artificial intel- ligence for disaster management.
